title: Astoria band, boyhood Chicago nightlife, and Armstrong borrowing a trumpet
summary: Barker describes playing with Jones and Collins' Astoria Band, peeking into Chicago cabarets as a boy in 1923, then Armstrong sitting in at the Royal Garden on a borrowed horn and the owner's anger.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Excuse me Danny, what was the name of the band you were with then?

I was with Lee Collins, Jones and Collins. Astoria Band. We played at Astoria. We played in New Orleans on Rampart Street which was owned by Beansy Furrier. It had once been owned by, I can't think of a man's name. It was a brewery people. Beansy took it over. It was a gambling concession. and we worked there. And Professor Cook was the emcee in musical and performance director and everything. He was the wheel around there. So he staged this train excursion to Chicago, and we had our band to play. I had been to Chicago in 23 as a kid to visit my aunt. And me and my little uncle, we used to sneak around in the nightclubs and peep through the side windows, lay on our stomachs and look down in the cellars at the people bawling like, you know, 8 o'clock in the morning, you know, and look down at the cabarets. And naturally, being from a musical family, we knew about this club. One particular was called Idlewild, which was on State Street. And a guy named Ollie Powell, Ollie Powell, he worked there. He was a singing drummer. He was a big favorite. He and Tony Jackson around Chicago during that period. I was about, see, 21, 22, 23, I was around. I was about 12, 13 years old. I had a little uncle. He was 14, 15. He and I were real tight. That's Paul's younger brother. The drummer, he played trumpet, and I picked up the guitar, ukulele, the guitar, and banjo, and guitar later. And we would stroll. We'd get up early, like, you know, 6.30 in the morning, and we'd go walk the streets looking for pennies and nickels, seeing this walk to gutters. And pick up, man, you know, 50, 60 cents apiece. People drop money on the sidewalk. And he had eagle eyes, man. He could spot money. The father of me says, keep your eye on watch, and we see pennies and nickels. State Street was very populous with black people seeing, you know, money. Okay. So we used to go and peep in this particular cabaret. It was in the cellar, and the window was just about a foot above, say, two feet above, ground level. On the side entrance, we'd go there on our stomachs and look down in the nightclub at the people. Everybody boozed up down there, and you could cut the smoke in there. You know, you could see, and you'd see this drumming entertainers, how they were acting. They couldn't see us, but we could see them, see. And we'd lay down looking. And there was new us coming from New Orleans that time in the morning. Our parents didn't know, they'd see where we were going. My uncle would say, let's go and look at the cabaret. So we'd go down the state, I think, in 46th Street. And there was this club. And we'd go around the side and look down and lay on our stomach maybe about 40, 50 minutes. And we'd be watching the hustlers and the underworld characters with the chicks shaking and taking money off the tables between their legs, you know, the pop bottle deal. And, well, that's the Chicago I'd seen then. And then Louis Armstrong came to the Royal Garden that night when we arrived and I'm sitting on the bandstand. And there was another band that was playing there. It was two bands. The Union, you had the Baha'i Union Band. It was a Chicago band playing about eight pieces and our band. It was somewhat of a battle of music. But we was playing this new old funk and New Orleans music and them people were dancing to it and they would sit out when the other band would play. No, I don't need a match. I'm just a habit. Louis came in, man, and he sat at the table which was seated right in front of the, right in front of the bandstand and intermission. We all met him and everybody, all the hustlers, all the racketeers and all the pimps and all the cats that were doing good from New Orleans with their cheeks. There was, Chicago's a fast town. A lot of underworld activity and nightlife and people who live, you know, a fast life. And particularly the ones who had migrated from Storyville, Black Red Light District went to New Orleans and they were up there finger-popping, talking loud, drawing the crowd, you know, flashing money. and they all were around Louis' table and they begged Louis to play. And Louis said, well, yeah, okay, give me the horn. So I'm sitting there and there's this guy's trumpet there. He said, hammer that horn, my boy. Boom, down, hammer that horn. So I had him, I just picked up the horn and handed him the horn. So he picked up the horn and said, what you gonna play? He sat down at, he stood up at the table he was at, in front of us, down. We were up on a high bandstand about four or five feet high. And Louis was in the table below. And, uh, they, somebody howled out a player, uh, uh, When You Smilin', which was a big hit at that time. So he went into When You Smilin', he played it. And he didn't have a mic, but the band was real soft and he sang it. And the house went in their uproar, man, about, you know, like, seven, 800 people to a thousand people to scream for more. And he played something else. And then he handed me back the horn. So I put the horn back. So after that, man, there was pandemonium in the house begging to play more and all the catch cards. So, Lee Kahn said, let's get off the bandstand. So while I'm getting off, this trumpet player came on and he said, who gave Louis Armstrong my horn? He didn't say it loud. I said, I ain't no horn. He said, well, God damn, who gave you permission to let him blow my horn? I don't let nobody blow my horn. I don't care who it was. If it was Gabriel, nobody blows my horn, nobody puts their lips on my mouthpiece. I don't know where people's mouth been at. One of them kind of things, see? So, I said, well, excuse me, the lawyer asked me for the horn. And I didn't think it was, to me, it was like, you know, the greatest thing ever could happen to play the horn because that horn was never blowed before, since, you know, the horn must have been felt real good after Armstrong blew it if it had any, if we're having feelings of having been blowed by the boss, the king.
